## Irish General Election Gender Breakdown, 2016–2020

Data visualisation in R: vote share, candidates fielded and candidates elected by gender in the 2016 and 2020 Irish general elections, using candidate data from the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage.

Originally written in 2021 as coursework (TU Dublin, MSc Computer Science — Data Science). The analysis is unchanged; the assignment framing and student number have been removed, and the data now loads from local files in `data/` instead of the original live URLs.

### Notes on this file

- The data files in `data/` are the candidate lists for the 2016 and 2020 general elections as published by the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage.
- Candidate counts in the text are counts after cleaning (rows with a missing result were dropped), not the official totals.
- The waffle chart in Insight 3 covers the top five parties only, not all elected TDs.
# 2.Pre-Processing	

### Loading Data 

```{r}
## Pre loading all library packages
library(ggpubr)
library(dplyr)
library(car)
library(psych)
library(Hmisc)
library(ggplot2)
library(gmodels)
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
## Reading the candidate datasets from data/ (originally downloaded from
## the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage open data portal)

geData20 <- read.csv('data/candidates-2020.csv', stringsAsFactors=FALSE, fileEncoding="latin1")
head(geData20)

geData16 <- read.csv('data/candidates-2016.csv', stringsAsFactors=FALSE, fileEncoding="latin1")
head(geData16)

```

#### 2.Pre-Processing	

### Cleaning Data

## NA values in dataset

```{r}

## Values in Result column has empty/missing values
## When I tried to identify missing values as NA it didn't work
## I assigned blank spaces as NA 

geData20[geData20==""]<- NA
geData16[geData16==""]<- NA

## Then returned data with FALSE and TRUE for NA values
geData20$Result
is.na(geData20$Result)

geData16$Result
is.na(geData16$Result)

## I want to omit NA values later when I review breakdown of gender and elected
na.omit(geData20$Result)
na.omit(geData16$Result)

geData20<- na.omit(geData20)
geData16<- na.omit(geData16)

```

##Columns data and new info in datasets

```{r}
# Get column names
colnames(geData20)
colnames(geData16)

# Changing columns in 2016 dataset to match 2020 dataset for consistency 
names(geData16)[names(geData16) == "Party"] <- "Party.Id"
names(geData16)[names(geData16) == "Gender"] <- "Gender.Id"

# Changing column in 2020 dataset to match 2016 dataset for consistency 
names(geData20)[names(geData20) == "Firstname"] <- "First.Name"

# Adding new columns with the year in preparation for merging both datasets
geData20["Year"] = "2020"
geData16["Year"] = "2016"

```


## Values cleanup and prepartion for merge 
 
```{r}
## Changing name of values to be include special characters 
geData20$Party.Id[geData20$Party.Id =="Fianna Fï¿½il"] <- "Fianna Fáil"
geData20$Party.Id[geData20$Party.Id =="Sinn Fï¿½in"] <- "Sinn Fein"
geData20$Party.Id[geData20$Party.Id =="Aontï¿½"] <- "Aontú"
geData20$Party.Id[geData20$Party.Id =="Green Party/ Comhaontas Glas"] <- "Green Party"
geData20$Party.Id[geData20$Party.Id =="The National Party - An Pï¿½irtï¿½ Nï¿½isiï¿½nta"] <- "The National Party"
geData20$Party.Id[geData20$Party.Id =="Solidarity - People Before Profit"] <- "People Before Profit"


## Changing name of values to be include special characters and be consistent with 2020 dataset

#geData16$Party.Id[geData16$Party.Id =="Fianna F·il"] <- "Fianna Fáil"
#geData16$Party.Id[geData16$Party.Id =="Sinn FÈin"] <- "Sinn Fein"
geData16$Party.Id[geData16$Party.Id =="Green Party/ Comhaontas Glas"] <- "Green Party"
geData20$Party.Id[geData20$Party.Id == "Anti-Austerity Alliance - People Before Profit"] <- "People Before Profit"

geData16$Party.Id

## Change values to be consistent for abbreviations

geData16$Party.Abbreviation[geData16$Party.Abbreviation =="AAA-PBP"] <- "P.B.P."


geData20$Party.Abbreviation[geData20$Party.Abbreviation =="S.P.B.P."] <- "P.B.P."


```

##Merging both datasets 

```{r}
geData <- rbind(geData20, geData16)

# Votes column is character 
geData$Votes <- as.numeric(as.character(geData$Votes))  # Convert string to numeric 

geData
```

### Data Deep Dive

# Section 1: Vote Share By Gender and Year	

There were 503 candidates in the 2020 General Election. There were 154 Females (30.6%) fielded for the 2020 Irish General Election compared to 349 Males (69.4%). 

```{r}
Hmisc::describe(geData20)
```

There were 268 candidates in the 2016 General Election. There were 88 Females (32.8%) fielded for the 2016 General Election compared to 180 Males (67.2%). 
```{r}
Hmisc::describe(geData16)
```

Below, we see a tabled full breakdown of how many candidates each party or non-party candidates fielded during the 2020 Irish General Election:

```{r}
## Get summary of the number of candidates fielded by each party
## Organized in ascending order to identify quickly top parties
sort(table(geData$Party.Abbreviation), decreasing = FALSE)
```

## INSIGHT 1 - Vote Share By Gender and Year

Looking at our entire dataset, without party lines. There were 161 Females (30%) fielded for the 2020 Irish General Election compared to 370 Males (70%). 

```{r}
table(geData$Gender.Id)
```

Barchart showing differences in the number of candidates by gender:
```{r}
df <- geData %>%
  group_by(Gender.Id) %>% # grouping and ordering in alphabetical order
  summarise(counts = n())
df

ggplot(geData , aes(Gender.Id)) + 
   geom_bar(aes(fill = Gender.Id)) + # colour consistent across all graphs
   ggtitle('Summary Of Candidates') + # titling graph
   labs(y="Number of Candidates", x = "Party") + # labelling x and y
   theme(axis.text=element_text(size=5), legend.position = "none") # smaller font to fit party abbreviations 
# removed the legend because it's cluttering the graph

```
Using descriptive statistics, we see the Median for Female candidates (2957.19) is different than Male candidates (3441). Indicates there is a positive skew to the right (1.98) for votes for Female candidates and for Male Candidates (1.28).

```{r}
## Summarize median of votes by gender and yer
geData %>% group_by(Gender.Id,) %>% summarise(median(Votes))
```

```{r}
#Iteration 4.1

geData %>% 
   ggplot(aes(Votes, colour=factor(Gender.Id))) + 
   geom_density(aes(y=..scaled..)) + 
   ggtitle('Vote Share by Gender in Both Elections') + labs(y="Scale", x = "Number of Votes")  +
   facet_wrap(~Year, scale="fixed") + 
   scale_color_discrete(name="Gender",labels = c("Female", "Male")) 
```
Plotting breakdown of gender and vote share shows a number of outliers for both Females and Males. 

It's clear that there is a higher vote share among Males with a higher median compared to Female candidates. 

An explanation for this could be related to the number of Female candidates (30%) versus Male candidates (70%) meaning the larger vote share is down purely to numbers.

```{r}
## Plotting Gender and Votes 
qplot(data = geData, x = Gender.Id, y = Votes, geom = 'boxplot', show.legend = FALSE,
 varwidth=TRUE,
 fill=Gender.Id,
 main="Vote Share Among Gender in 2020 and 2016",
 xlab="Gender",
 ylab="Votes")

qplot(data = geData20, x = Gender.Id, y = Votes, geom = 'boxplot', show.legend = FALSE,
 varwidth=TRUE,
 fill=Gender.Id,
 main="Vote Share Among Gender in 2020",
 xlab="Gender",
 ylab="Votes")

qplot(data = geData16, x = Gender.Id, y = Votes, geom = 'boxplot', show.legend = FALSE,
 varwidth=TRUE,
 fill=Gender.Id,
 main="Vote Share Among Gender in 2016",
 xlab="Gender",
 ylab="Votes")
```
```{r}
## Plotting in one plot
ggplot(geData, aes(x= Year, y=Votes, fill=Gender.Id)) + 
    geom_boxplot() +
    facet_wrap(~Gender.Id)
```
```{r}
# Iteration conveying both genders by year
ggplot(geData, aes(x=Year, y=Votes, fill=Gender.Id)) + 
    geom_boxplot() +
    facet_wrap(~Year, scale="free") + 
   ggtitle('Vote Share Among Gender in 2016 and 2020') + labs(y="Number of Votes", x = "Year of General Election") + 
   scale_fill_discrete(name = "Gender", labels = c("Female", "Male"))
```

```{r}

# Final iteration conveying votes bu gender with a fixed scale
ggplot(geData, aes(x=Year, y=Votes, fill=Gender.Id)) + 
    geom_boxplot() +
    facet_wrap(~Gender.Id, scale="fixed") + 
   ggtitle('Vote Share Among Gender in 2016 and 2020', subtitle = 'Female candidates received just 30% votes compared to Male candidates at 70%') + labs(y="Number of Votes", x = "Year of General Election") + 
   scale_fill_discrete(name = "Gender", labels = c("Female", "Male"))


```

Female candidates received an average of 2503 votes compared to Male candidates with 3441 votes. 
```{r}
geData %>% group_by(Gender.Id) %>% summarise(median(Votes))
```

Female candidates received, on average, around 65% (2016) or 61% (2020) the number of votes that Male candidates received in the 2020 Irish General Election. 
```{r}
4216 * 100 / 6469 #2016
3708.5 * 100 / 6035.5 #2020
```



## INSIGHT #2 - Candidates Fielded by Gender by Top Five Parties

For the purpose of this analysis, we will focus on the top 5 parties who received the highest vote share in the 2020 Irish General Election versus the total number of candidates fielded, where relevant.

Given the number of outliers, we will use the median of votes. For this purpose we will select: FF (5753), FG (5456), LAB (2208), SF (12539), GP (3650). 

```{r}
## Summarize median of votes by party
geData %>% group_by(Party.Abbreviation) %>% summarise(median(Votes))
```

Checking data to determine parties which received the highest portion of votes. The range of votes received by SF surpass any other party. 
```{r}
## Assigning new data frame with the top five parties
geDatatop <- filter(geData, Party.Abbreviation %in% c('F.F.', 'F.G.', 'G.P.','LAB.', 'S.F.'))
table(geDatatop$Gender.Id)

geDatatop20 <- filter(geData20, Party.Abbreviation %in% c('F.F.', 'F.G.', 'G.P.','LAB.', 'S.F.'))
table(geData20$Party.Abbreviation)

geDatatop16 <- filter(geData16, Party.Abbreviation %in% c('F.F.', 'F.G.', 'G.P.','LAB.', 'S.F.'))
table(geData16$Party.Abbreviation)
```

Plotting the top five parties. We see SF hast a higher vote share than any other party, despite only fielding half (42) the number of candidates compared to FF (82) and FG (81).
```{r}

geData %>% group_by(Party.Abbreviation, Year) %>% summarise(median(Votes))


## Top five parties
## Plotted visually in ascending order of vote share
qplot(data = geDatatop, reorder(Party.Abbreviation, Votes), y = Votes, geom = 'boxplot',
 varwidth=TRUE, show.legend = FALSE,
fill=Party.Abbreviation,
 main="Vote Share Among Top Parties in Both Elections", subtitle = 'Male candidates outweighed female candidates 2-1 in F.F. and F.G. in both elections ',
 xlab="Party",
 ylab="Votes") +
    facet_wrap(~Year, scale="fixed") + 
   scale_fill_discrete(name = "Gender", labels = c("Female", "Male"))

```

Below, we see a breakdown of the number of Female and Male candidates fielded by each of the top 5 parties.

```{r}
## Table 
table(geDatatop$Gender.Id, geDatatop$Party.Abbreviation, geDatatop$Year)
```

In 2012, Ireland introduced a 30% gender quota for party candidates at general elections. We can see that each of the top parties reached that quota with FF and FG just passing the quota. 
```{r}

# 2016
14 * 100 / 40 # FF
12 * 100 / 39 # FG
8 * 100 / 22 # GP
8 * 100 / 18 # LAB
11 * 100 / 29 # SF

# 2020
25 * 100 / 75 # FF
23 * 100 / 77 # FG
14 * 100 / 35 # GP
10 * 100 / 31 # LAB
14 * 100 / 40 # SF
```

When we plot the breakdown of gender, we can see that candidates are largely Male across the party spectrum, accounting for 60 - 70% of candidates.

```{r}
## Creating histogram to share breakdown of Female and Male candidates by party
## Changing labels
ggplot(geDatatop, aes(Party.Abbreviation, ..count..)) +
   geom_bar(aes(fill = Gender.Id), position = "dodge") + 
   ggtitle('Candidates For Top Parties By Gender') + 
   labs(y="Number of Candidates", x = "Party") + 
   theme(axis.text=element_text(size=10)) +
    facet_wrap(~Gender.Id, scale="fixed") + 
   scale_fill_discrete(name = "Gender", labels = c("Female", "Male"))

## Creating histogram to share breakdown of Female and Male candidates by party
## Changing to convey breakdown of both by year instead
ggplot(geDatatop, aes(Party.Abbreviation, ..count..)) +
   geom_bar(aes(fill = Gender.Id), position = "dodge") + 
   ggtitle('Candidates for Top Parties by Gender in 2016 and 2020', subtitle = 'Male candidates outweighed female candidates 2-1 in F.F. and F.G. in both elections ') + 
   labs(y="Number of Candidates", x = "Party") + 
   theme(axis.text=element_text(size=10)) +
    facet_wrap(~Year, scale="fixed")
```

## INSIGHT 3 - Candidates Elected by Gender	

Number of candidates elected or excluded based on total number of votes by Gender. More Male candidates were Elected than Female candidates.  

```{r}
# Using the cleaned up data for Result with missing values
# Excluding all the missing values 
geData <- filter(geData, Party.Abbreviation %in% c('F.F.', 'F.G.', 'G.P.','LAB.', 'S.F.'))
table(geData$Result, geData$Gender.Id, geData$Year)
```

Plotting the data emphasizes the difference even further. With 30 - 40% of candidates being Female, we only saw 20% of candidates elected to Dáil Éireann being Female.
```{r}
## Creating histogram to share breakdown of Female and Male candidates elected and excluded by party
ggplot(geDatatop, aes(Result, ..count..)) + 
   geom_bar(aes(fill = Gender.Id), position = "dodge") + 
   ggtitle('Candidates Elected or Excluded For Top Parties By Gender') + 
   labs(y="Number of Candidates", x = "Elected To Dáil Éireann") + 
   theme(axis.text=element_text(size=10)) 


## Creating histogram to share breakdown of Female and Male candidates by party and by year
## Changing labels
ggplot(geDatatop, aes(Result, ..count..)) + 
   geom_bar(aes(fill = Gender.Id), position = "dodge") + 
   ggtitle('Candidates Elected or Excluded For Top Parties By Gender', subtitle = 'More men are elected as TDs than women') + 
   labs(y="Number of Candidates", x = "Elected To Dáil Éireann") + 
   theme(axis.text=element_text(size=10)) +
   facet_wrap(~Year, scale="fixed") + 
   scale_fill_discrete(name = "Gender", labels = c("Female", "Male"))

```
Below we have plotted the total number of candidates who were elected to Dáil Éireann in the 2020 Irish General Election across every party and non-party. SF eleted 
```{r}
# Using the cleaned up data for Result with missing values
# Excluding all the missing values 
geDataElected <- filter(geData, Result == 'Elected')
geDataElected16 <- filter(geData16, Result == 'Elected')
geDataElected20 <- filter(geData20, Result == 'Elected')

# Tabling the values for a quick sense check
library(janitor)
tabyl(geDataElected$Party.Abbreviation, sort = TRUE) # Ordered alphabetically to be consistent in report
tabyl(geDataElected16$Party.Abbreviation, sort = TRUE) # Ordered alphabetically to be consistent in report
tabyl(geDataElected20$Party.Abbreviation, sort = TRUE) # Ordered alphabetically to be consistent in report

table(geDataElected$Party.Abbreviation, geDataElected$Gender.Id, geDataElected$Year)
table(geDataElected$Gender.Id, geDataElected$Year)

16 * 100 / 71 # Total % of female TDs in 2016
26 * 100 / 137 # Total % of female TDs in 2020

```

Plotting candidates elected by top parties combined from two elections.
```{r}

# Plotting this table onto a graph
ggplot(geDataElected, aes(Party.Abbreviation, ..count..)) + 
   geom_bar(aes(fill = Party.Abbreviation), position = "dodge") + # consistent colours in all graphs
   ggtitle('Candidates Elected in Top Parties in Both Elections') + # titling graph
   labs(y="Number of Candidates", x = "Party") + # naming labels
   theme(axis.text=element_text(size=5), legend.position = "none") # changing font size to fit onto plot
```
Plotting candidates elected in the two elections for insight 3.
```{r}

geDataTopElected <- filter(geDataElected, Party.Abbreviation %in% c('F.F.', 'F.G.', 'G.P.','LAB.', 'S.F.'))
table(geDataTopElected$Party.Abbreviation, geDataTopElected$Gender.Id, geDataTopElected$Year)
# Plotting this table onto a graph

ggplot(geDataElected, aes(Party.Abbreviation, ..count..)) + 
   geom_bar(aes(fill = Gender.Id), position = "dodge") + # consistent colours in all graphs
   ggtitle('Candidates Elected for Top Parties in 2016 and 2020', subtitle = 'More women elected in 2020 than 2016, but men still outnumber women in 2020') + # titling graph
   labs(y="Number of Candidates", x = "Party") + # naming labels
   theme(axis.text=element_text(size=5))  +
   facet_wrap(~Year, scale="fixed") + 
   scale_fill_discrete(name = "Gender", labels = c("Female", "Male")) 

```
